info.name: Trends Bird — Ecommerce Admin API
info.description:
Admin API for the Trends Bird backend intern assignment.

## Getting started
1. Run the API (`npm run dev`) and seed the database (`npm run seed`).
2. Open **Authentication → Login (super admin)** and send it. The access token is saved to the `accessToken` collection variable automatically.
3. Every other request uses `Authorization: Bearer {{accessToken}}`.

## Checking 403 behaviour
Send **Authentication → Login (limited catalog user)**. That saves `catalogToken`.
The requests in the **Access control checks** folder use it to prove that a low-privilege token is refused on permission, role and user routes — including the delete routes.

## Token strategy
The API's primary strategy is HttpOnly cookies; `Authorization: Bearer` is accepted as a documented fallback so this collection needs no cookie or CSRF setup. If you prefer cookies, enable Postman's cookie jar and drop the Authorization header — you will then also need to send the `csrfToken` cookie value in an `X-CSRF-Token` header on every mutating request.

item.name: Authentication
item.description:
Login, refresh with rotation, real logout, session.

Order matters when running the whole folder: the super-admin login and refresh come first, because logging in as the catalog user replaces the cookie jar's session.

request.description:
Saves `{{accessToken}}` and `{{csrfToken}}`. Also sets the accessToken, refreshToken and csrfToken cookies.

The refresh token is never returned in the body - only as an HttpOnly cookie.

exec: pm.test('no password hash in the response', () => pm.expect(pm.response.text()).to.not.include('$2b$'));
pm.test('no refresh token in the body', () => pm.expect(pm.response.text()).to.not.include('"refreshToken"'));

request.description: Returns the user, their role, and a flat array of permission names. The dashboard renders from this.

Cookie-driven, so it echoes the CSRF token in the `X-CSRF-Token` header - exactly what the dashboard does. Without that header this returns 403.

A new refresh token is issued and the old one is revoked. Presenting an already-rotated token revokes the whole chain - reuse detection.

Run this once after logging in. It fills the permission-id variables the Role and User examples use, so the whole collection can be executed top to bottom in the Collection Runner without hand-editing ids.

Saves `{{catalogToken}}`. This account has catalog access only - no permission, role or user rights.

It also replaces the cookie-jar session, which is why it runs after the refresh request above.
Returns the same message as a wrong email, so the form cannot be used to discover which accounts exist.

exec: pm.test('message is Invalid email or password.', () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().message).to.eql('Invalid email or password.'));

request.description: Naming a group `Catalog Discount` and ticking Create produces `catalog-discount:create`. Action names are normalised: `"  Create "` and `"CREATE"` both become `create`.

item.name: Edit a group (actions are the desired end state)

request.description: Renaming the group renames every permission inside it. Any action missing from `actions` is removed — that is how the permission grid submits.
A capability outside the standard set. `Bulk Import` normalises to `bulk-import`.
The flat list the role grid ticks against.
The permission goes and the role links go with it, so no role is left pointing at a missing record. The response reports how many roles were affected.

item.name: Create a role and grant permissions in one step

request.description: Pass `grantAll: true` instead of `permissionIds` for an administrator role.

exec: if (pm.response.code === 201) { const body = pm.response.json(); pm.collectionVariables.set('roleId', body.data.id); }

request.description: Returns every permission so the edit screen can pre-tick the grid.
A revoked permission takes effect on the holder's very next request, not at their next token refresh.
Refused with 409 while any user still holds it, and refused if it would leave nobody able to manage roles.

item.name: User
item.description: Dashboard accounts. Each holds exactly one role.

request.description: Search by name or email; filter by role and status. All server-side.
`roleId` is required and never defaulted. Omitting it returns 422 naming the field.
A deactivated user can neither log in nor refresh, and their existing tokens stop working immediately.
Soft delete: the row is kept with `isDeleted`, excluded from reads, and the email stays reserved.

item.name: Media
item.description: Shared library. One asset attaches to many products.

request.description:
Content is validated by decoding the bytes — the extension and the client's Content-Type are ignored. A text file renamed `.png` is rejected with 422. SVG is deliberately not accepted (inline script).

Every image gets a generated 400px WebP thumbnail. Batch uploads are all-or-nothing.

formdata.description: Pick one or more images. Field name is `files`; `file` also works.

request.description: `type` filters to IMAGE or VIDEO.
409 if any user avatar, category image, brand logo, attribute value or product attachment still references it.
Detaches every reference, then removes the record, the stored file and its thumbnail.
The real nested tree with a `depth` on every node — what the parent picker renders from.
Nesting is unlimited: Electronics > Phones > Android and deeper.
A category can never become its own ancestor. Rejected at any depth, not just the direct case.
Refused with 409 while it still has children — nothing is orphaned.

item.name: Brand
item.description: One brand per product, many products per brand.

request.description: Refused with 409 while products still reference it.

item.name: Attribute
item.description: The dimensions a product varies along.

request.description: A COLOR_SWATCH value must carry `colorCode`. Omitting it returns 422; passing a `mediaId` instead also returns 422.
An IMAGE_SWATCH value must carry `mediaId`.
Changing `type` re-validates every existing value, so a type change cannot silently invalidate them.
Values are unique within their attribute — `Red` may exist under Colour and separately under another attribute.
Refused with 409 once a product variant uses it — deleting it would corrupt every variant built on it.
Refused with 409 while variants or products use it.

item.name: Product
item.description: The centre of the catalog: simple or variable.

request.description: Each row carries thumbnail, brand, categories, and a flat `price` or a `priceRange` computed from effective (sale) prices.
Price, sale price and stock live on the product. `stockStatus` is derived from the count.

item.name: Create a VARIABLE product with variants (atomic)

request.description:
The whole create is one transaction — if a variant fails validation, no half-built product survives.

Two variants with the same attribute combination are rejected with 409, including when the ids are listed in a different order.

item.name: Reject: price on a variable product (422)

request.description: The `hasVariants` flag drives validation in both directions: a price on a variable product and a variant on a simple one are both rejected.

item.name: Get one product (everything the edit screen needs)

request.description: Categories, brand, media, variants and each variant's attribute values.
Produces every combination, skipping any that already exist. Pass `replaceExisting: true` to rebuild from scratch. Capped at 200 combinations.

item.name: Attach media (product, variant or attribute value)

request.description: Attaching to an attribute value is how picking Red shows the right photos without duplicating them on every Red variant.

item.name: Set the thumbnail (demotes the previous one)

request.description: Never two thumbnails at once — enforced by a partial unique index in PostgreSQL, not only in application code.
Variants and media attachments go with it, but the media assets themselves survive — other products may use them.

item.name: Access control checks
item.description: Run 'Login (limited catalog user)' first. Every request here must return 403 — and the ones with no token must return 401.

request.description: A malformed token is rejected with 401. The Authorization header is read before any cookie, so this stays a 401 even if a session cookie is present in the jar.
Correctly structured JWT signed with the wrong key. Rejected with 401.

Send this from a fresh client with no cookie jar. Authentication is applied to the whole /api/v1 tree, so even an unknown path returns 401 rather than 404.

NOTE: in the Collection Runner this returns 403 instead, because Postman replays the session cookie set by the earlier login and the catalog user simply lacks `user:read`. Both answers prove the route is guarded.

exec: pm.test('denied (401 without cookies, 403 with the catalog session)', () => pm.expect([401, 403]).to.include(pm.response.code));

item.name: Session teardown (run last)
item.description: These two requests end the current session on purpose, so they sit at the end of the collection. Running them mid-collection would break every folder above.

request.description: Revokes every session for this user, including the current one. Re-run `npm run seed` afterwards to restore the documented password.
Cookie-driven, so it echoes the CSRF token in the `X-CSRF-Token` header. The refresh token stops working immediately. Clearing a browser cookie alone would not achieve this.
